title: Unbounded Self Adjoint Operators and Stones Theorem

items.title: Unbounded linear operator: domain, graph and extension
items.statement: A (possibly unbounded) linear operator on a complex Hilbert space $H$ is a linear map $T:D(T)\subseteq H\to H$ whose domain $D(T)$ is a linear subspace and is part of the data. Its graph is $\Gamma(T)=\{(x,Tx):x\in D(T)\}\subseteq H\oplus H$, and for operators $S,T$ one writes $S\subseteq T$ when $\Gamma(S)\subseteq\Gamma(T)$; equality $S=T$ requires $D(S)=D(T)$ and equal values. The orthogonal sum $H\oplus H$ carries the norm $\|(x,y)\|=(\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2)^{1/2}$, and $T$ is closed when $\Gamma(T)$ is closed in $H\oplus H$.
items.strategy: Fix the conventions that the domain is part of the operator and that the inner product is linear in the first variable. Present the graph inside the orthogonal direct sum and record the graph-norm formula used by the closure, core and adjoint statements. No choice principle is used beyond the given Hilbert-space data.
items.axiom_audit: Choice-free relative to the Hilbert space $H$ and the linear map $T$.

references.title: Dana P. Williams, Lecture Notes on the Spectral Theorem
Theo Buehler and Dietmar A. Salamon, Functional Analysis

items.title: Densely defined, closed, closable operators and cores
items.statement: A linear operator $T$ on $H$ is densely defined when $D(T)$ is dense in $H$; closed when $\Gamma(T)$ is closed in $H\oplus H$; closable when it admits a closed extension. A subspace $D_0\subseteq D(T)$ is a core for a closed $T$ when it is dense in $D(T)$ for the graph norm $\|x\|_T=(\|x\|^2+\|Tx\|^2)^{1/2}$, equivalently when the closure of $\Gamma(T|_{D_0})$ equals $\Gamma(T)$.
items.strategy: Restate the notions through the graph norm: prove that $\|\cdot\|_T$ is a norm on $D(T)$, that $T$ is closed exactly when $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$ is complete when $H$ is complete, and that a core is a graph-dense subspace. Countable Choice is used only to select one graph point in each shrinking ball when completeness is used to prove closedness; the core equivalence is transferred topologically by the graph isometry.
items.axiom_audit: Assumes Countable Choice exactly for complete subspace implies closed; the closed-to-complete direction and the graph-homeomorphism proof of the core equivalence are choice-free.

items.title: Closure of a closable operator
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. An operator $T$ is closable if and only if $x_n\in D(T)$, $x_n\to0$ and $Tx_n\to y$ imply $y=0$. In that case the closure of $\Gamma(T)$ is the graph of an operator $\overline T$, called the closure of $T$; it is the least closed extension of $T$, and $T$ is closed if and only if $\overline T=T$.
items.strategy: The displayed condition is exactly single-valuedness of the graph closure: a pair $(0,y)$ with $y\ne0$ in $\overline{\Gamma(T)}$ contradicts single-valuedness, and conversely the closure of a subspace is a subspace, so it is the graph of an operator precisely when it meets the second coordinate axis only at $0$. Minimality among closed extensions is immediate from the definition of closure in $H\oplus H$. Use the graph and graph-norm language of the two preceding items.
items.axiom_audit: Uses Countable Choice exactly to read closure in the metric space $H\oplus H$ as sequential closure; declared as a dependency.

references.title: Dana P. Williams, Lecture Notes on the Spectral Theorem

items.title: Adjoint of a densely defined operator
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $T$ be densely defined. Then $y\in D(T^*)$ when the map $x\mapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle$ is bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$; because $D(T)$ is dense this bounded functional has a unique representing vector $T^*y\in H$ with $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,T^*y\rangle$ for all $x\in D(T)$. This defines the adjoint $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$ of $T$.
items.strategy: Extend the bounded functional uniquely from the dense subspace to $H$ and apply Hilbert Riesz representation to obtain existence of $T^*y$; uniqueness of the representing vector uses nondegeneracy of the inner product. Record explicitly that only ambient-norm boundedness on $D(T)$ is required, so no extension or closure of $T$ is presupposed.
items.axiom_audit: Uses Countable Choice exactly through Hilbert Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]); declared as a dependency.

references.title: Dana P. Williams, Lecture Notes on the Spectral Theorem

items.title: The adjoint is well defined, closed, and reverses inclusions
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For a densely defined $T$ the adjoint $T^*$ is well defined and linear, $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace, $T^*$ is closed, $\operatorname{ran}(T-z)^\perp=\ker(T^*-\bar z)$ for every $z\in\mathbb C$, and $S\subseteq T$ implies $T^*\subseteq S^*$ whenever both adjoints are defined.
items.strategy: Well-definedness and linearity follow from the definition and continuity of the inner product. For closedness let $y_n\in D(T^*)$ with $y_n\to y$ and $T^*y_n\to w$; then $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\lim\langle Tx,y_n\rangle=\lim\langle x,T^*y_n\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle$ for every $x\in D(T)$, so $y\in D(T^*)$ and $T^*y=w$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]] plus density). The kernel-range identity is the definition of the adjoint read backwards, and monotonicity follows from the graph inclusion.
items.axiom_audit: Countable Choice is inherited from the adjoint definition; no further choice is used.

references.title: Dana P. Williams, Lecture Notes on the Spectral Theorem
Theo Buehler and Dietmar A. Salamon, Functional Analysis

items.title: Closability is equivalent to density of the adjoint domain
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For a densely defined $T$ the following are equivalent: $T$ is closable, and $D(T^*)$ is dense in $H$. In that case $\overline T=T^{**}$ and $T^*=\overline T^{\,*}$. In particular every symmetric operator is closable.
items.strategy: Identify the graph of the adjoint: $\Gamma(T^*)=V(\Gamma(T))^\perp$ for the unitary $V(y,x)=(-x,y)$ of $H\oplus H$. If $D(T^*)$ is dense then $\Gamma(T^{**})=V(V\Gamma(T)^\perp)^\perp=\overline{\Gamma(T)}$, so the graph closure is a graph; conversely a vector of $D(T^*)^\perp$ produces an element $(0,w)$ of $\Gamma(\overline T)=\Gamma(T)$, hence $w=0$. Use the double orthogonal complement theorem for linear subspaces and the closedness of $T^*$.
items.axiom_audit: Inherits Countable Choice through [[thm-double-orthogonal-complement-is-closure]] and the adjoint construction; nothing stronger.

references.title: Dana P. Williams, Lecture Notes on the Spectral Theorem
Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition

items.title: Symmetric, self-adjoint, and essentially self-adjoint operators
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. A densely defined operator $T$ is symmetric when $T\subseteq T^*$, self-adjoint when $T=T^*$ (equal domains and values), and essentially self-adjoint when its closure $\overline T$ is self-adjoint. Every symmetric operator is closable, its closure is symmetric, and a self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension inside $H$.
items.strategy: Symmetry is a graph inclusion, so it is preserved by closure: $T\subseteq T^*$ with $T^*$ closed gives $\overline T\subseteq T^*$, hence $T^{**}=\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$ by monotonicity and the identity $\overline T=T^{**}$. Closability of a symmetric $T$ follows since $T^*$ is closed. The last claim is the chain $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$.
items.axiom_audit: Inherits Countable Choice from the adjoint construction ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]]).

references.title: Dana P. Williams, Lecture Notes on the Spectral Theorem
Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition
Theo Buehler and Dietmar A. Salamon, Functional Analysis

items.title: A symmetric closed operator that is not self-adjoint
items.statement: Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. On $H=L^2(0,1)$ let $T=-i\,d/dx$ with domain $D(T)=\{f\in AC[0,1]:f'\in L^2(0,1),\ f(0)=f(1)=0\}$. Then $T$ is densely defined, closed and symmetric, $D(T^*)=\{g\in AC[0,1]:g'\in L^2(0,1)\}$, and $T^*g=-ig'$. Hence $T\ne T^*$: there are densely defined closed symmetric operators that are not self-adjoint, and $T^*$ is a proper closed extension of $T$ that is itself not symmetric, while the periodic domain $\{g\in AC[0,1]:g'\in L^2,\ g(0)=g(1)\}$ carries a closed symmetric extension strictly between $T$ and $T^*$.
items.strategy: Identify unique AC representatives. Prove interval test-function density by explicit endpoint cutoffs and a two-term L2 error bound. Closedness of the zero-boundary derivative follows from uniform convergence of its primitives. Compute the maximal adjoint with k=H+ig and test k-its mean against the zero-mean derivative space. Compute the periodic adjoint by testing its boundary form with the constant function, giving self-adjointness and closedness. Constants and the coordinate function witness both strict inclusions.
items.axiom_audit: Countable Choice and Dependent Choice are used exactly through the published absolutely continuous calculus suppliers ([[thm-integration-by-parts-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]], [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]]) and the $L^2$ density of test functions; declared.

items.title: Resolvent and spectrum of an unbounded operator
items.statement: For a linear operator $T$ on $H$ the resolvent set is $\rho(T)=\{z\in\mathbb C: z-T:D(T)\to H$ is bijective and $(z-T)^{-1}\in B(H)\}$, and $\sigma(T)=\mathbb C\setminus\rho(T)$. For $z\in\rho(T)$ one writes $R_T(z)=(z-T)^{-1}$ (this library's convention, matching the bounded resolvent of FA-15). If $\rho(T)\ne\emptyset$ then $T$ is closed.
items.strategy: Use the shift zI-T. Recover D(T)=ran R and TRy=zRy-y. Prove the graph of the bounded inverse closed as the zero set of the continuous map (v,w) -> w-Rv, then transport it by the explicit homeomorphism (v,w) -> (w,zw-v). No closed graph theorem or sequential characterization of closed sets is used. Distinguish the zero space from the zero operator on a nonzero space.
items.axiom_audit: Choice-free. The closedness of $T$ when the resolvent set is nonempty is proved from the closed graph of the bounded inverse, not from the closed graph theorem, so no choice principle is imported by this definition.

references.title: Dana P. Williams, Lecture Notes on the Spectral Theorem
Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition
Theo Buehler and Dietmar A. Salamon, Functional Analysis

items.title: Resolvent of a self-adjoint operator: nonreal resolvents and the estimate
items.statement: For a self-adjoint operator $T$ one has $\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb R\subseteq\rho(T)$, and for $z=a+ib$ with $b\ne0$ the resolvent satisfies the identity $\|(T-z)x\|^2=\|(T-a)x\|^2+b^2\|x\|^2$ for $x\in D(T)$ and the bound $\|R_T(z)\|\le1/|\operatorname{Im}z|$. Consequently $\sigma(T)\subseteq\mathbb R$.
items.strategy: Expand $\|(T-z)x\|^2$ and cancel the cross terms using $T\subseteq T^*$, obtaining (7.6) of the source; this makes $T-z$ injective with closed range and bounded inverse on its range. Density of the range holds because $\operatorname{ran}(T-z)^\perp=\ker(T^*-\bar z)=\{0\}$ by the self-adjoint closed-kernel argument; closedness of $T$ upgrades dense range to all of $H$. Then $z\in\rho(T)$ with the stated bound.
items.axiom_audit: Inherits Countable Choice from the self-adjointness and adjoint suppliers; no further choice, and no closed graph theorem is used (the bound is proved directly).

references.title: Dana P. Williams, Lecture Notes on the Spectral Theorem
references.locator: Theorem 7.34, estimate (7.6) and its proof, pp.35–36

items.title: Range criterion for self-adjointness
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined symmetric operator. Then the following are equivalent: (a) $T$ is self-adjoint; (b) $T$ is closed and $\ker(T^*-z)=\{0\}$ for all nonreal $z$; (c) $T$ is closed and $\ker(T^*\mp i)=\{0\}$; (d) $\operatorname{ran}(T-z)=H$ for all nonreal $z$; (e) $\operatorname{ran}(T\pm i)=H$; (f) $\sigma(T)\subseteq\mathbb R$. In particular a closed symmetric operator is self-adjoint if and only if $\operatorname{ran}(T\pm i)=H$, and the same criterion holds with $i$ replaced by $i\lambda$, $\lambda>0$.
items.strategy: Follow the source's cycle of implications: (a)$\Rightarrow$(b) is the symmetry computation of the resolvent estimate; (b)$\Rightarrow$(d) uses $\operatorname{ran}(T-z)^\perp=\ker(T^*-\bar z)$ together with the estimate and closedness; (d)$\Rightarrow$(e) is immediate; (e)$\Rightarrow$(a) takes $v\in D(T^*)$, solves $(T-i)w=(T^*-i)v$ by surjectivity, and tests against $\operatorname{ran}(T+i)=H$ to conclude $v=w\in D(T)$; (f)$\Rightarrow$(b) and (c)$\Rightarrow$(e) are formal.
items.axiom_audit: Inherits Countable Choice from the adjoint and self-adjointness suppliers; no further choice.

references.title: Dana P. Williams, Lecture Notes on the Spectral Theorem
Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition
Theo Buehler and Dietmar A. Salamon, Functional Analysis

items.title: Cayley transform of a self-adjoint operator
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. For a self-adjoint operator $T$ the Cayley transform is $C_T=(T-i)(T+i)^{-1}=I+2iR_T(-i)$. It is a unitary operator on $H$ with $C_T^*=(T+i)(T-i)^{-1}=C_T^{-1}$ and $\ker(I-C_T)=\{0\}$; further $I-C_T=2i(T+i)^{-1}$ and $I+C_T=2T(T+i)^{-1}$ on $D(T)$.
items.strategy: The factors $(T\mp i)$ are surjective with bounded inverses by the range criterion, so $C_T$ is a bounded everywhere-defined operator; compute $C_T^*C_T=I$ using $R_T(z)^*=R_T(\bar z)$ so that $C_T$ is unitary, and $I-C_T=2iR_T(-i)=2i(T+i)^{-1}$ is injective. The displayed formulas for $I\pm C_T$ are the algebraic identities used by the inverse construction.
items.axiom_audit: Inherits Countable Choice from the resolvent and adjoint suppliers; nothing further.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition
Theo Buehler and Dietmar A. Salamon, Functional Analysis

items.title: Cayley correspondence between self-adjoint operators and unitaries
items.statement: The map $T\mapsto C_T$ is a bijection from the set of self-adjoint operators on $H$ onto the set of unitary operators $U$ with $\ker(I-U)=\{0\}$. The inverse assigns to such $U$ the operator with domain $D(T)=\operatorname{ran}(I-U)$ and action $T(I-U)y=i(I+U)y$; for this $T$ one has $T-i$ onto and $T+i$ onto, so $T$ is self-adjoint, and $C_T=U$.
items.strategy: Forward direction from the preceding definition. For the converse, define $T$ on $\operatorname{ran}(I-U)$ by the displayed formula (well-defined and single-valued because $\ker(I-U)=0$) and verify symmetry by expanding $\langle i(I+U)y,(I-U)y\rangle$ using unitarity; then show $T\pm i$ are onto with $D(T)=\operatorname{ran}(I-U)$, so the range criterion makes $T$ self-adjoint and $C_T=U$. All identities are checked in the library's resolvent convention $R_T(z)=(z-T)^{-1}$.
items.axiom_audit: Inherits Countable Choice from [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]] and the adjoint construction; declared.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition
Theo Buehler and Dietmar A. Salamon, Functional Analysis

items.title: Integral of a measurable function against a projection-valued measure
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be $\Sigma$-measurable. Put $D(f(E))=\{x\in H:\int_X|f|^2\,dE_x<\infty\}$, where $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$, and define $f(E)x=\lim_n\int f\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}\,dE\,x$ for $x\in D(f(E))$. The domain and the values depend only on the class of $f$ modulo $E$-null sets.
items.strategy: Define the zero-space calculus directly as the unique operator. Otherwise use the bounded measurable PVM calculus. Prove domain linearity by scalar-measure bounds, and Cauchy convergence by the uniform tail bound |f_n-f_m|^2 <= |f|^2 1_{|f|>N} for n,m>=N and dominated convergence. Hilbert completeness gives the limit. Equal measurable representatives off an E-null set have equal domains and equal truncation vectors by the quadratic identity.
items.axiom_audit: Countable Choice is inherited from [[thm-pvm-integral-is-a-star-homomorphism]] and the PVM infrastructure; declared.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition
Theo Buehler and Dietmar A. Salamon, Functional Analysis

items.title: The unbounded PVM integral is densely defined, closed and normal
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a projection valued measure on $(X,\Sigma)$
on the complex Hilbert space $H$ and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be $\Sigma$-measurable. Then the
operator $f(E)$ of [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]] is densely defined
and closed, and it is normal, in the sense $D(f(E))=D(f(E)^*)$ and equal norms for the operator and its adjoint; in particular $D(f(E))=D(\overline f(E))$ and
$\|f(E)x\|=\|\overline f(E)x\|$ for all such $x$. Moreover
$$\|f(E)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x,\qquad \langle x,f(E)x\rangle=\int\overline f\,dE_x\qquad(x\in D(f(E))),$$
and $(f(E))^*=\overline f(E)$; in particular $f(E)$ is self-adjoint whenever
$f$ takes real values. Finally, if $(g_n)$ are bounded $\Sigma$-measurable functions with
$|g_n|\le C|f|$ pointwise and $g_n\to f$ pointwise, then $g_n(E)x\to f(E)x$
for every $x\in D(f(E))$.
items.strategy: Treat H={0} directly. For nonzero H prove the scalar identities, a bounded-minus-unbounded error identity and dominated approximation, bounded multiplier measure transfer, density by spectral cutoffs, both adjoint inclusions, then closedness by applying the adjoint identity to conjugate f. All pairings use the first-variable-linear convention.
items.axiom_audit: Inherits Countable Choice from the PVM calculus; the limit arguments use only scalar dominated and monotone convergence.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition

items.title: Spectral theorem for unbounded self-adjoint operators (PVM form)
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every self-adjoint operator $T$ on a nonzero complex Hilbert space $H$ has a unique regular projection-valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ with $D(T)=\{x:\int\lambda^2dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\}$ and $Tx=\int\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x$ for $x\in D(T)$. Conversely, for every regular PVM $E$ on $\mathbb R$ the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint, and its spectral PVM is $E$ again.
items.strategy: Route chosen: Cayley plus the bounded spectral theorem. The Cayley transform $C_T$ is unitary, so by the bounded PVM form it has a unique regular spectral PVM $F$ on the unit circle; $\ker(I-C_T)=0$ gives $F(\{1\})=0$, and transporting along the homeomorphism $\psi(\lambda)=(\lambda-i)(\lambda+i)^{-1}$ of $\mathbb R$ onto $S^1\setminus\{1\}$ defines $E=F\circ\psi$. The calculus identities $1-C_T=2iR_T(-i)$ and $T(1-C_T)=i(1+C_T)$ show that the unbounded integral $A=\int\lambda\,dE$ equals $T$ on $D(A)=D(T)=\operatorname{ran}(1-C_T)$. Uniqueness: for any regular PVM $E'$ representing $T$, the bounded calculus gives $\int\psi\,dE'=C_T$, so the pushforward of $E'$ is a bounded spectral PVM of $C_T$ and equals $F$ by the bounded uniqueness theorem, hence $E'=E$. The converse is the closedness/self-adjointness part of [[lem-unbounded-pvm-integral-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to real $\lambda$. Williams's resolvent route (using $R_T(i)$ and its cyclic decomposition) is an alternative and is recorded as a remark, not used.
items.axiom_audit: Uses full AC through the bounded normal spectral theorem and its uniqueness theorem (both declared there); the transport step itself is choice-free.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition
Dana P. Williams, Lecture Notes on the Spectral Theorem
references.locator: Theorem 7.35 (alternative resolvent route, complete proof), pp.36–37

references.title: Theo Buehler and Dietmar A. Salamon, Functional Analysis

items.title: Unbounded Borel functional calculus: domains, products, spectral mapping
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $H$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let
$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be Borel. Write $u(T)=u(E)$, with the truncation definition below. If $H=\{0\}$, use its unique PVM and unique full-domain operator directly. Then:

1. $f(T)^*=\overline f(T)$;
2. $f(T)g(T)$ has domain $D(g(T))\cap D((fg)(T))$ and equals the restriction of
   $(fg)(T)$ to that domain, and its closure is $(fg)(T)$;
3. on $D(f(T))\cap D(g(T))$ the sum $f(T)+g(T)$ equals the restriction of
   $(f+g)(T)$, and the closure of $f(T)+g(T)$ is $(f+g)(T)$;
4. the spectrum of $f(T)$ is the essential range
   $\{z\in\mathbb C:E(f^{-1}(B_\varepsilon(z)))\ne0$ for every
   $\varepsilon>0\}$ of $f$ with respect to $E$;
5. if $f$ is continuous then that essential range is the closure of
   $f(\sigma(T))$, with the closure redundant when $f(\sigma(T))$ is closed.
items.strategy: Prove scalar measure transfer and general square-dominated approximation from bounded truncations. Establish exact sum and product domains and actions. For the product graph core truncate |g|; for the sum truncate both |f| and |g|. Construct the bounded inverse using the piecewise reciprocal 1/(z-f) and prove both inverse domains. Prove the converse using unit vectors in small spectral preimages. Apply the criterion to the identity function and disjointify a countable rational-interval zero-projection cover; continuity gives the final image-closure formula. Handle the zero space directly.
items.axiom_audit: Inherits AC from the unbounded spectral theorem; no additional choice.

items.title: Strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group
items.statement: A strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group on $H$ is a map $U:\mathbb R\to B(H)$ with $U(0)=I$, $U(s+t)=U(s)U(t)$ for all $s,t$, each $U(t)$ unitary, and $t\mapsto U(t)x$ continuous for every $x\in H$. Continuity at $t=0$ alone suffices, and weak continuity is equivalent to strong continuity for unitary families.
items.strategy: Use metric-map continuity from the usual metric on the real parameter line to the norm metric on $H$. Prove that continuity of $t\mapsto U(t)x$ at $0$ extends to all $t$ by the group law and isometry, and that weak continuity at $0$ implies strong continuity at $0$ from the squared-norm identity; Cauchy--Schwarz proves the reverse implication. No choice principle is used.
items.axiom_audit: Choice-free.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition

items.title: Infinitesimal generator of a unitary group
items.statement: For a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group $U$ the infinitesimal generator is $Gx=\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t\bigl(U(t)x-x\bigr)$ with domain $D(G)$ the set of $x$ for which the limit exists in $H$. $D(G)$ is a linear subspace and $G$ is linear; the self-adjoint generator convention of this page is $T=-iG$, so that $U(t)=e^{itT}$.
items.strategy: Define the two-sided real-parameter derivative by its punctured epsilon-delta norm condition, equivalently by continuity at zero after extending the quotient there. Record the maximal domain, prove linearity on the same punctured parameter, and fix the sign convention $T=-iG$ with its translation to Teschl's convention. No choice principle is used.
items.axiom_audit: Choice-free.

references.locator: Section 1.1, generator definition before Proposition 1.10, pp.5–6

items.title: A self-adjoint operator generates a strongly continuous unitary group
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be self-adjoint with spectral PVM $E$ and put $U(t)=e^{itT}=\int e^{it\lambda}\,dE(\lambda)$. Then $U$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group, $U(t)D(T)=D(T)$, $TU(t)=U(t)T$ on $D(T)$, and the derivative $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(U(t)x-x)$ exists exactly for $x\in D(T)$, where it equals $iTx$; thus the generator is $G=iT$.
items.strategy: Group law and unitarity come from the scalar identities for $e^{it\lambda}$ and the functional calculus. Strong continuity is dominated convergence applied to $\int|e^{it\lambda}-e^{it_0\lambda}|^2dE_x$. For the domain: if $x\in D(T)$ then $\int|\frac1t(e^{it\lambda}-1)-i\lambda|^2dE_x\to0$ by dominated convergence using $|e^{i\lambda t}-1|\le|t\lambda|$; conversely, if the difference quotients converge to $z$ then Fatou's lemma applied to $\int|\frac1t(e^{it\lambda}-1)|^2dE_x$ along a sequence $t\to0$ gives $\int\lambda^2dE_x<\infty$, so $x\in D(T)$, and the limit is $iTx$ by uniqueness. Invariance of $D(T)$ follows from the calculus with the multiplier $\lambda e^{it\lambda}$.
items.axiom_audit: Inherits AC from the unbounded Borel calculus; dominated convergence and Fatou are the only measure-theoretic inputs.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition
Dana P. Williams, Lecture Notes on the Spectral Theorem
Roland Schnaubelt, Evolution Equations (lecture notes)

items.title: Laplace resolvents of a unitary group
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $U$ be a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary
group on $H$ with infinitesimal generator $G$, and let $\lambda>0$. Then
$$Q_\pm(\lambda)x=\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}U(\pm t)x\,dt$$
is a Bochner integral depending linearly and boundedly on $x$, with
$\|Q_\pm(\lambda)\|\le1/\lambda$ and $\operatorname{ran}Q_\pm(\lambda)\subseteq
D(G)$; moreover
$$(\lambda\mp G)Q_\pm(\lambda)=I,\qquad Q_\pm(\lambda)(\lambda\mp G)=I\ \text{on }D(G),$$
and $Q_+(\lambda)+Q_-(\lambda)=2\lambda\,Q_+(\lambda)Q_-(\lambda)$.
items.strategy: Explicit simple approximants and scalar exponential integral give Bochner existence and bound. Translate the integral to obtain the right derivative; the group law turns it into a two-sided derivative. Unitarity implies Re<Gx,x>=0 and hence injectivity of lambda +/- G. The right inverse and injectivity give the left inverse on its exact domain. Finish with the signed algebraic sum identity.
items.axiom_audit: Countable Choice is consumed by the compact integration bridge and Bochner framework. The existing Dependent Choice hypothesis is retained but not additionally needed; no half-line FTC is used.

items.title: The generator of a unitary group is closed and skew-adjoint
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. The generator $G$ of a strongly continuous
one-parameter unitary group $U$ is densely defined, closed, and
skew-adjoint: $G^*=-G$. Consequently $T=-iG$ is self-adjoint with $D(T)=D(G)$.
items.strategy: Laplace approximate identity gives density by a near-zero/tail norm estimate. Differentiating the preserved inner product gives skew-symmetry. For closedness use x_n=Q_+(1)(x_n-Gx_n), or the resolvent closedness interface. Correctly signed shifted ranges T+i=i(1-G), T-i=-i(1+G) give self-adjointness of T=-iG. Compute the scalar adjoint with equality of domains to conclude G*=-G.
items.axiom_audit: Countable Choice and Dependent Choice are propagated from the Laplace supplier; the compact integration bridge and adjoint/range suppliers use Countable Choice. No arbitrary-index choice is introduced.

items.title: Stone's theorem: unitary groups and self-adjoint generators
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. The map $T\mapsto U(t)=e^{itT}$ is a bijection from self-adjoint operators on $H$ onto strongly continuous one-parameter unitary groups, with $U(t)=e^{itT}$ computed by the Borel calculus of $T$. Its inverse assigns to $U$ the generator $G$ and the self-adjoint operator $T=-iG$; $D(T)=D(G)$ is exactly the set of vectors at which $t\mapsto U(t)x$ is differentiable at $0$, and $(U(t)x-x)/t\to iTx$ there.
items.strategy: Surjectivity and the derivative characterisation are the preceding two lemmas. Injectivity: if $e^{itT_1}=e^{itT_2}$ for all $t$ then the generators agree, hence $T_1=T_2$; the generator is determined by the group. State both directions with the convention $U(t)=e^{itT}$ and translate Teschl's $e^{-itA}$ explicitly.
items.axiom_audit: Inherits AC from the Borel calculus direction and Countable Choice from the Laplace-resolvent direction.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition
Dana P. Williams, Lecture Notes on the Spectral Theorem
Roland Schnaubelt, Evolution Equations (lecture notes)

items.title: Deficiency subspaces and deficiency indices
items.statement: Assume full AC. For a densely defined closed symmetric operator on a complex Hilbert space, define K_+=ker(T*-i), K_-=ker(T*+i) and their well-defined orthonormal-basis cardinal dimensions. The Cayley partial isometry has initial complement K_+ and final complement K_-.
items.strategy: Prove the symmetric norm identity by first-variable-linear expansion, then closedness of both ranges and orthogonal decompositions. Prove basis cardinal independence with Bessel and AC. Specify the Cayley domain and the complementary unitary maps.
items.axiom_audit: Full AC for orthonormal bases and simultaneous support enumerations/assignments in infinite cardinal comparison; supplies all countable-choice interfaces.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition
Dana P. Williams, Lecture Notes on the Spectral Theorem

items.title: Von Neumann parameterization of self-adjoint extensions
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined closed symmetric operator on a complex Hilbert space H, with first-variable-linear inner product,
with deficiency subspaces $K_\pm$ ([[def-deficiency-subspaces-and-deficiency-indices]]),
and let $V:K_+\to K_-$ be a unitary operator. Then
$$D(T_V)=D(T)\oplus\{u+Vu:u\in K_+\},\qquad T_V(x+u+Vu)=Tx+iu-iVu$$
defines a self-adjoint extension $T_V$ of $T$; the sum is direct and $D(T_V)$
is dense. The map $V\mapsto T_V$ is a bijection from the set of unitary
operators $K_+\to K_-$ onto the set of self-adjoint extensions of $T$.
items.strategy: Assemble U=C_T direct-sum (-V) using the orthogonal range decompositions. Dense ran(I-U) contains D(T); unitary invariance of inner products excludes fixed vectors. Apply the inverse Cayley correspondence, prove the direct domain sum by injectivity of I-U, and compute the action on each summand. For an arbitrary extension prove that its Cayley transform maps both orthogonal complements onto one another, recover V with a minus sign, then prove uniqueness. Include zero deficiency spaces and empty parameter sets.
items.axiom_audit: Full AC inherited from the deficiency-space interface, including its Hilbert-dimension convention; AC implies CC for the Cayley correspondence. The construction from a supplied V makes no new family of choices.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition
Theo Buehler and Dietmar A. Salamon, Functional Analysis

items.title: Existence of self-adjoint extensions is equality of deficiency indices
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. A densely defined closed symmetric operator $T$ has a self-adjoint extension if and only if $d_+(T)=d_-(T)$. It is self-adjoint if and only if $d_+=d_-=0$. A densely defined symmetric (but possibly non-closed) $S$ is essentially self-adjoint if and only if $d_\pm(\overline S)=0$, equivalently $\ker(S^*\mp i)=\{0\}$; if $d_+(\overline S)=d_-(\overline S)$ then $S$ has self-adjoint extensions.
items.strategy: If the dimensions are equal, Hilbert bases of $K_+$ and $K_-$ (maximal orthonormal families exist by Zorn) give a unitary $V:K_+\to K_-$, and the parameterization yields an extension. Conversely any self-adjoint extension restricts to a unitary $K_+\to K_-$, so the dimensions agree; and $d_+=d_-=0$ is self-adjointness by the range criterion. For closable symmetric $S$ apply the closed case to $\overline S$ and use that $S^*=(\overline S)^*$ and $\ker(S^*\mp i)=\ker((\overline S)^*\mp i)$.
items.axiom_audit: Uses full AC for the existence of orthonormal bases of the deficiency subspaces ([[thm-existence-of-a-maximal-orthonormal-family]]); declared, and heredity from [[thm-hilbert-space-with-a-given-orthonormal-basis-is-ell-two-of-the-index-set]] is Countable Choice.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition
Theo Buehler and Dietmar A. Salamon, Functional Analysis

items.title: Pure point, absolutely continuous and singular continuous spectral subspaces
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be self-adjoint with spectral PVM $E$ and scalar measures $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$; on the zero Hilbert space use the unique zero PVM directly. Then $H_{\mathrm{pp}}=\{x:E_x$ is purely atomic$\}$, $H_{\mathrm{ac}}=\{x:E_x\ll\lambda\}$ (Lebesgue measure) and $H_{\mathrm{sc}}=\{x:E_x$ is atomless and singular$\}$; $0$ belongs to all three. For each type one sets $\sigma_{\mathrm{type}}(T)=\sigma(T|_{H_{\mathrm{type}}})$; $\sigma_{\mathrm{pp}}$ is the closure of the set of eigenvalues and need not equal the point spectrum, and the three sets $\sigma_{\mathrm{type}}$ may overlap.
items.strategy: Use the nonzero-space spectral theorem when $H$ is nonzero and the unique zero PVM directly when $H$ is zero. Define the three classes of finite Borel measures on $\mathbb R$ through their declared unique decomposition; note that a purely atomic measure, a measure absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, and an atomless singular measure are mutually exclusive up to the zero measure, so the definitions are meaningful. Record the vector $0$ and the convention $\sigma_{\mathrm{type}}(T)=\sigma(T|_{H_{\mathrm{type}}})$ with the restrictions constructed in the next theorem.
items.axiom_audit: Inherits AC through the spectral theorem this definition is built on; the measure-theoretic classification itself relies on the published Lebesgue decomposition theorem, which declares AC.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition

items.title: Canonical decomposition into pure point, absolutely continuous and singular continuous parts
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a self-adjoint operator $T$ with spectral PVM $E$ the sets $H_{\mathrm{pp}},H_{\mathrm{ac}},H_{\mathrm{sc}}$ are closed, mutually orthogonal, $T$-reducing subspaces with $H=H_{\mathrm{pp}}\oplus H_{\mathrm{ac}}\oplus H_{\mathrm{sc}}$, canonically determined by $T$; the corresponding restrictions are self-adjoint and have purely atomic, absolutely continuous, and atomless singular spectral measures respectively. If $H$ is separable, then for a maximal scalar spectral measure $\mu$ with disjoint Borel supports $B_{\mathrm{pp}},B_{\mathrm{ac}},B_{\mathrm{sc}}$ of its three Lebesgue components one has $H_{\mathrm{type}}=\operatorname{ran}E(B_{\mathrm{type}})$.
items.strategy: Split each scalar measure on disjoint Borel carriers; domination preserves types. Prove linearity and norm closure by scalar projection estimates and countable carrier unions. Mutual singularity gives orthogonality. Project each vector onto its scalar carriers to obtain the exhaustive canonical sum. Show commutation with every spectral projection, domain invariance and unbounded truncation commutation. Restrict the regular PVM to prove self-adjointness. For every supplied maximal finite measure, domination gives the carrier projection formula. Zero subspaces handled directly.
items.axiom_audit: Full AC inherited from spectral and measure decomposition interfaces; countable carrier choices in closure and countable-union countability explicit. No arbitrary-index cyclic model is used.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition

items.title: Relative boundedness with respect to an operator
items.statement: Let $A$ be a linear operator. An operator $B$ is $A$-bounded when $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and there are finite constants $a,b\ge0$ with $\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|$ for all $x\in D(A)$; the infimum of the admissible $a$ is the $A$-bound (relative bound) of $B$. One says the $A$-bound is below one when some $a<1$ is admissible.
items.strategy: Record that the graph norm of $A$ controls $B$ exactly when $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and $B$ is bounded for the graph norm, and that the two formulations are equivalent (with adjusted constants). Note that relative boundedness is defined for an arbitrary linear $A$, needs no closedness, and that the constant $b$ is not intrinsic. Use the $A$-bound terminology consistently in the perturbation block.
items.axiom_audit: Choice-free.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition

items.title: Second resolvent identity for a closed perturbation
items.statement: Let $A$ and $C$ be closed operators with $D(C)=D(A)$, let $B=C-A$, and assume $B$ is bounded for the graph norm of $A$. Then for $z\in\rho(A)\cap\rho(C)$ the second resolvent identity holds: $R_C(z)-R_A(z)=-R_A(z)BR_C(z)=-R_C(z)BR_A(z)$, every product being interpreted on its natural domain, which is all of $H$.
items.strategy: Since $R_A(z)$ and $R_C(z)$ map $H$ into $D(A)=D(C)$ and $B:C\to H$ is graph-norm bounded, both compositions are everywhere defined and bounded. Compute $R_C(z)+R_A(z)BR_C(z)=R_A(z)(C-z)R_C(z)=R_A(z)$ and reverse the roles of $A$ and $C$; the closedness of the two operators is what makes the resolvents well defined.
items.axiom_audit: Choice-free: closedness of $A$ and $C$ makes both resolvents bounded everywhere-defined operators, and the identity is operator algebra. No choice principle is used.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition

items.title: Kato–Rellich theorem
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Work on a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first variable. Let $A$ be self-adjoint and let $B$ be symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and
$A$-bound less than one ([[def-relative-boundedness-with-respect-to-an-operator]]).
Then $A+B$ with domain $D(A)$ is self-adjoint. If $A$ is merely essentially
self-adjoint and $B$ is symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and $A$-bound less
than one, then $A+B$ on $D(A)$ is essentially self-adjoint and its closure is
the self-adjoint operator obtained by applying the first part to $\overline A$
and the graph-norm extension of $B$ to $D(\overline A)$. If $A\ge\gamma$ and
$(a,b)$ is an admissible pair for $B$ with $a<1$, then
$A+B\ge\gamma-\max\{a|\gamma|+b,\ b/(1-a)\}$.
items.strategy: Use (z-A-B)=(I-BR_A(z))(z-A) at both imaginary shifts and the range criterion. Derive spectral lower bounds from scalar projection supports. Construct every real resolvent below gamma-max(a|gamma|+b,b/(1-a)) and apply that support equivalence. Extend B restricted to D(A) by graph limits for the essentially self-adjoint case.
items.axiom_audit: AC explicitly inherited from spectral calculus and countable graph-approximation choices; implies the range criterion Countable Choice.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition

items.title: Discrete and essential spectrum of a self-adjoint operator
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a self-adjoint operator $A$ the discrete spectrum $\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)$ is the set of eigenvalues that are isolated points of $\sigma(A)$ with finite-dimensional eigenspace; the essential spectrum is $\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)=\sigma(A)\setminus\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)$, and it is closed. Equivalently, with $P$ the spectral measure of $A$: $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)$ iff $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue and $\operatorname{rank}P((\lambda-\varepsilon,\lambda+\varepsilon))<\infty$ for some $\varepsilon>0$, and $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ iff $\operatorname{rank}P((\lambda-\varepsilon,\lambda+\varepsilon))=\infty$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.
items.strategy: Use the scalar squared-norm identity to identify the singleton projection with the eigenspace, including its domain. A rank-r interval cannot contain r+1 spectral points, by disjoint nonzero projections. Support then makes every spectral point in a finite-rank interval an isolated eigenvalue. Derive both rank characterizations and closedness by nesting.
items.axiom_audit: Inherits AC through the spectral theorem required for the spectral-projection characterization; the set-theoretic definition alone needs none.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition
references.locator: Section 6.4, (6.29)-(6.30), p.170; local projection proof supplied here

references.title: Theo Buehler and Dietmar A. Salamon, Functional Analysis

items.title: Weyl criterion for the essential spectrum
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a self-adjoint operator $A$ and real $\lambda$, one has $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ if and only if there is a sequence $x_n\in D(A)$ with $\|x_n\|=1$, $x_n\rightharpoonup0$ weakly, and $\|(A-\lambda)x_n\|\to0$. The sequence may be chosen orthonormal; such a sequence is called a singular Weyl sequence for $\lambda$.
items.strategy: For every real lambda, finite-rank interval projections contradict a unit weakly-null residual sequence by the spectral complement estimate. Conversely use DC on finite lists, beginning with the empty list, to choose orthonormal vectors in infinite-rank intervals of radius 1/(n+1). Prove domain membership from bounded spectral support and weak nullity using Bessel and Riesz.
items.axiom_audit: AC inherited from spectral theorem, implies DC for successive vector choices and Countable Choice for Hilbert Riesz. No separability assumption.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition

items.title: Relative compactness with respect to an operator
items.statement: Assume full AC. Let A be self-adjoint on a complex Hilbert space and B:D(A)->H linear and graph-norm bounded. B is A-compact when BR_A(z) is compact for one, equivalently every, z in rho(A). Such B form a vector space and have A-bound zero (an infimum, not necessarily attained).
items.strategy: Derive both resolvent product orders from inverse identities on D(A). For bound zero use h_n(mu)=(i-mu)/(in-mu), strong convergence of it and its conjugate via DCT, then compactness on weakly null test vectors to prove ||BR_A(in)|| tends to zero.
items.axiom_audit: Full AC for the spectral theorem, countable witness choices and the compact weak-to-norm supplier.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition
references.locator: Section 6.4, the definition before Lemma 6.21 and Lemma 6.21, pp.172–173

references.title: Theo Buehler and Dietmar A. Salamon, Functional Analysis

items.title: Weyl's theorem: invariance of the essential spectrum
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. If self-adjoint $A,C$ have compact resolvent difference $R_A(z)-R_C(z)$ for one nonreal $z$ (equivalently for every common resolvent point), then $\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)=\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(C)$. In particular a bounded self-adjoint compact perturbation preserves the essential spectrum, and if $K$ is symmetric and $A$-compact then $\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A+K)=\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ on $D(A+K)=D(A)$.
items.strategy: Let $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ with singular Weyl sequence $x_n$. From $R_A(z)-\frac1{\lambda-z}=\frac1{z-\lambda}R_A(z)(A-\lambda)$ and $\|(A-\lambda)x_n\|\to0$ get $(R_A(z)-\frac1{\lambda-z})x_n\to0$; compactness of the resolvent difference and weak convergence $x_n\rightharpoonup0$ (compact operators send weakly null sequences to norm null sequences) give $(R_C(z)-\frac1{\lambda-z})x_n\to0$, hence $(C-\lambda)R_C(z)x_n\to0$. Since $\|R_C(z)x_n\|\to|\lambda-z|^{-1}>0$, the normalized images are a singular Weyl sequence for $C$, so $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(C)$; interchange the roles. Parameter independence is the resolvent identity. For the perturbation clause, the second resolvent identity writes the resolvent difference as $-R_{A+K}(z)KR_A(z)$, a product with the compact operator $KR_A(z)$; when $K$ is only $A$-compact one uses Kato–Rellich to know $A+K$ is self-adjoint and the identity $KR_{A+K}(z)=KR_A(z)(I+BR_{A+K}(z))$ with the Neumann inverse to transfer compactness.
items.axiom_audit: Inherits AC from the Weyl criterion and the compact-operator suppliers; Kato–Rellich is used for the self-adjointness of the perturbed operator.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition
references.locator: Theorem 6.19 with proof, Lemma 6.21 and Lemmas 6.22–6.23, pp.171–174

items.title: Norm and strong resolvent convergence
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $A_n,A$ be self-adjoint operators on the same Hilbert space $H$. One says $A_n\to A$ in the norm resolvent sense when $R_{A_n}(z)\to R_A(z)$ in operator norm for one nonreal $z$, and in the strong resolvent sense when $R_{A_n}(z)\to R_A(z)$ in the strong operator topology for one nonreal $z$. The independence of the choice of nonreal $z$ is a theorem, not part of the definition.
items.strategy: Assume Countable Choice, fix $z_0\in\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb R$, and define both notions at $z_0$; the stated axiom licenses the self-adjoint resolvent estimate, hence $z_0\in\rho(A_n)\cap\rho(A)$ and the definition is meaningful. Record that parameter independence is proved later by the resolvent-star-algebra argument.
items.axiom_audit: Assumes Countable Choice explicitly because the cited self-adjoint resolvent estimate requires it.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition

items.title: The resolvent star algebra is dense in C_0(R)
items.statement: Fix $z\notin\mathbb R$ and let $A$ be the $*$-algebra generated by the single function $r(x)=(x-z)^{-1}$ in $C_0(\mathbb R)$. Then $A$ is uniformly dense in $C_0(\mathbb R)$. Consequently, if self-adjoint $A_n,A$ satisfy $R_{A_n}(z)\to R_A(z)$ strongly (respectively in norm) at one nonreal $z$, then the same convergence holds at every nonreal $z'$, in particular at $\bar z$.
items.strategy: Identify $\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}$ with the one-point compactification $S$ and extend $r$ by $r(\infty)=0$; every element of $A$ is a polynomial in $r$ and $\bar r$ and vanishes at $\infty$, so $A\subseteq C(S)$ is a self-adjoint complex function algebra whose only common zero is $\infty$ (since $r(x)\ne0$ on $\mathbb R$) and which separates points of $\mathbb R$ because $r$ is injective. The complex Stone–Weierstrass dichotomy therefore identifies the uniform closure of $A$ with $\{f\in C(S):f(\infty)=0\}=C_0(\mathbb R)$. For the consequence, use the resolvent identity $R(z')-R'(z')=[1+(z'-z)R(z)]^{-1}(R(z)-R'(z))[1+(z'-z)R'(z)]^{-1}$: the outer factors are bounded with norms controlled by $1+|z'-z|/|\operatorname{Im}z|$, strong/norm convergence is preserved under bounded left and right multiplication, and $1+(z'-z)R(z)=(z'-T)R(z)$ is invertible as a composition of the bijections $R(z):H\to D(T)$ and $(z'-T):D(T)\to H$.
items.axiom_audit: Inherits Countable Choice from the resolvent and spectral suppliers; the Stone–Weierstrass input is choice-free.

items.title: Continuous functional calculus under resolvent convergence
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $A_n,A$ be self-adjoint operators on a complex Hilbert space $H$ and
suppose $A_n\to A$ in the strong resolvent sense. Then
$f(A_n)x\to f(A)x$ for every bounded continuous $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ and
every $x\in H$. If $A_n\to A$ in the norm resolvent sense, then
$\|f(A_n)-f(A)\|\to0$ for every bounded continuous $f$ with
$\lim_{t\to+\infty}f(t)=\lim_{t\to-\infty}f(t)$. In both cases the conclusion
does not depend on the nonreal parameter used in the definition of convergence.
items.strategy: Treat zero H directly. Identify bounded reciprocal calculus with the resolvent on its exact domain. Prove parameter independence by D_n(w)=(I+(z-w)R_n(w))D_n(z)(I+(z-w)R(w)), with fixed right factor. Apply polynomial density only after both conjugate parameters converge; explicitly bound products and uniform approximation. Use explicit cutoffs and the four-term estimate for bounded continuous functions.
items.axiom_audit: Inherits AC from the Borel calculus; the truncation argument uses only the bounded Borel SOT convergence of the calculus.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition
references.locator: Theorem 6.31, Corollary 6.32 and Lemma 6.34 with proofs, pp.179–181

items.title: Unitary groups converge under strong resolvent convergence
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $A_n,A$ be self-adjoint operators on a complex Hilbert space $H$ with
$A_n\to A$ in the strong resolvent sense. Then
$$e^{itA_n}x\longrightarrow e^{itA}x\qquad\text{for every }t\in\mathbb R\text{ and every }x\in H.$$
If, in addition, $A$ and all $A_n$ are bounded below by a common real constant
$\gamma$ (meaning $\langle Sx,x\rangle\ge\gamma\|x\|^2$ for $x\in D(S)$ and $S=A,A_n$), then $e^{-tA_n}\to e^{-tA}$ strongly for every $t\ge0$.
items.strategy: Apply bounded continuous calculus to exp(it lambda) for arbitrary real t. For semigroups prove the spectral projection below the common quadratic-form lower bound vanishes, using bounded intervals and monotone convergence. Extend the exponential constantly below gamma and use equality off the null spectral set, including its full domain.
items.axiom_audit: Inherits AC from the two declared suppliers.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition
Roland Schnaubelt, Evolution Equations (lecture notes)
references.locator: Section 1.1 and Chapter 4, resolvent convergence orientation

items.title: Spectral form domain and core of a semibounded operator
items.statement: Assume AC. For a self-adjoint A bounded below by c, the domain of sqrt(A-c) and q_A[x]=c||x||²+||sqrt(A-c)x||² are independent of c. The form equals <Ax,x> on D(A), which is a core for the complete norm with squared weight 1+lambda-c. The form is closed and bounded below by c. Include the zero Hilbert space directly.
items.strategy: Prove E((-infinity,c))=0 by bounded spectral projections and the operator lower bound. Use finite scalar mass for shift independence. Symmetric spectral cutoffs give D(A) membership and convergence for weight 1+lambda-c. Closed graph of the square root gives completeness; write the associated Hermitian form explicitly.
items.axiom_audit: Inherits AC from the unbounded Borel calculus; the form argument is choice-free.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition
references.locator: Section 3.1, (3.52)–(3.53), and Section 4.4 form-domain discussion, pp.110 and 139–141

items.title: Min-max principle below the essential spectrum
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let A be a self-adjoint operator on a complex Hilbert space H, bounded below by c, with form domain Q(A) and form q_A of [[lem-spectral-form-domain-and-core-of-a-semibounded-operator]]. Put $\Lambda=\inf\sigma_{\rm ess}(A)$, with inf(empty)=+infinity. List the eigenvalues below Lambda in nondecreasing order with multiplicity as E_1,E_2,..., setting E_n=Lambda after the list is exhausted. Then for every integer n>=1,
$$E_n=\inf_{\substack{L\subseteq Q(A)\text{ linear}\\\dim L=n}}\ \sup_{\substack{x\in L\\\|x\|=1}}q_A[x]
=\sup_{\substack{F\subseteq Q(A)\text{ linear}\\\dim F\le n-1}}\ \inf_{\substack{x\in Q(A)\cap F^\perp\\\|x\|=1}}q_A[x].$$
All infima over empty sets are +infinity. Finite dimensions here are ordinary linear dimensions, equivalently Hilbert dimensions for these finite-dimensional subspaces. The second outer family is always nonempty, since it contains {0}. Whenever Q(A) contains an (n-1)-dimensional subspace, the same value is obtained by requiring dim F=n-1. The at-most convention includes the exhausted finite-dimensional case for all n without taking a supremum over an empty outer family.

The first infimum is unchanged if its trial spaces L are restricted to D(A). If E_n<Lambda, both outer values are attained, respectively by spans of the first n and the first n-1 orthonormal eigenvectors (the latter span is {0} when n=1).
items.strategy: Prove finite spectral counting below the essential threshold by compact interval covers. Establish beta<=alpha<=alpha_D by finite linear equations. For an eigenvalue use the first n and n-1 eigenvectors, removing only strictly lower eigenspaces. At a finite essential edge use infinite-rank bounded intervals to construct D(A) trial spaces. For exhausted empty essential spectrum identify finite-dimensional H and use empty-infimum conventions. At-most n-1 trial dimension handles all n; padding proves the exact-dimension variant whenever available.
items.axiom_audit: Full AC inherited from spectral/form suppliers and used for countable finite-eigenspace basis choices and a sequence approaching the essential infimum. Remaining choices are finite.

title: Unbounded Self Adjoint Operators and Stones Theorem — Examples

items.title: Multiplication operators: domain, spectral measure and spectrum
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure
space, let $m:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable and finite $\mu$-almost everywhere,
and on the Hilbert space $H=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]) put
$$D(M_m)=\Bigl\{f\in L^2(X,\mu):\int_X|m|^2|f|^2\,d\mu<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad M_mf=mf .$$
Then $M_m$ is self-adjoint; its spectral projection valued measure is
$E(B)=M_{\mathbf 1_{m^{-1}(B)}}$; for every Borel $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ its functional calculus is
$g(M_m)=M_{g\circ m}$ on the natural domain; and
$\sigma(M_m)$ equals the essential range
$\{t\in\mathbb R:\mu(m^{-1}(t-\varepsilon,t+\varepsilon))>0$ for every
$\varepsilon>0\}$.
items.strategy: Construct indicator projections and prove strong countable additivity by dominated convergence. Each scalar pushforward measure is finite Borel on the second-countable LCH real line, hence regular. Prove the pushforward integral identity from indicators, simple functions and MCT; compute bounded and unbounded integrals as multipliers. Apply the converse spectral theorem only after regularity, treating H={0} directly. Use sigma-finiteness to find a positive finite-measure subset and detect any nonzero indicator multiplier.
items.axiom_audit: AC supplies the spectral theorem and implies Countable Choice for complex L2 Hilbert completeness. Sigma-finiteness is used to detect positive-measure sets by nonzero L2 indicators; it is not required to define the null-class quotient.

references.title: Dana P. Williams, Lecture Notes on the Spectral Theorem
Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, second edition

items.title: Position operator on $L^2(\mathbb R)$
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. On $H=L^2(\mathbb R)$ let $Q$ be multiplication by $x$ with $D(Q)=\{f\in L^2:\int x^2|f(x)|^2dx<\infty\}$. Then $Q$ is self-adjoint, $\sigma(Q)=\mathbb R$, its spectral PVM is $E(B)f=\mathbf 1_Bf$, and $e^{itQ}f(x)=e^{itx}f(x)$ defines a strongly continuous unitary group whose generator is $iQ$ in the page's convention.
items.strategy: Specialize the multiplication-operator example to $(X,m)=(\mathbb R,x)$; the essential range of $x$ is $\mathbb R$, giving $\sigma(Q)=\mathbb R$. Identify the spectral projections with indicator multipliers and compute $e^{itQ}$ by the functional calculus; strong continuity and the generator statement are the corresponding clauses of the generation lemma. Record that $D(Q)$ is proper and dense, so $Q$ is unbounded.
items.axiom_audit: Inherits AC from the spectral theorem.

items.title: Periodic derivative and its unitary translation group
items.statement: Assume full AC. On complex L2(0,1), the periodic AC derivative P=-i d/dx is self-adjoint, V(t)f=f((x+t) mod 1)=e^{itP}f is strongly continuous unitary, and its derivative generator is G=iP with domain D(P).
items.strategy: First-linear integration by parts, explicit simultaneous formulas for P+epsilon i, unitary translation on equivalence classes, density of the minimal derivative domain, two-sided averaged-derivative L2 estimate, and maximality of the already self-adjoint P.
items.axiom_audit: Full AC for Stone and inherited Countable Choice/Dependent Choice in absolutely continuous calculus, density, range and compactness; explicit formulas select no additional family.

items.title: The minimal derivative has deficiency indices $(1,1)$ and many self-adjoint extensions
items.statement: Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $T$ be the minimal periodic-derivative operator of the previous counterexample, i.e. $T=-i\,d/dx$ on $D(T)=\{f\in AC[0,1]:f'\in L^2,\ f(0)=f(1)=0\}$ on $H=L^2(0,1)$. Then $d_+(T)=d_-(T)=1$: $K_+=\ker(T^*-i)=\mathbb C\,e^{-x}$ and $K_-=\ker(T^*+i)=\mathbb C\,e^{x}$, so the self-adjoint extensions of $T$ are exactly the operators $T_\theta$ whose domain is the absolutely continuous functions satisfying $f(1)=e^{i\theta}f(0)$; in particular $T$ itself is not self-adjoint and has infinitely many self-adjoint extensions.
items.strategy: Compute $T^*$ from the previous counterexample: $D(T^*)=\{g\in AC[0,1]:g'\in L^2\}$ with $T^*g=-ig'$; then $K_+$ and $K_-$ are the one-dimensional spans of $e^{-x}$ and $e^{x}$ respectively because $T^*g=\pm ig$ means $g'=\mp g$. Thus $d_+=d_-=1$ and the von Neumann parameterization identifies the extensions with the unitaries $\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$, i.e. the phases $e^{i\theta}$; translating the domain formula $D(T_V)=D(T)\oplus\{u+Vu\}$ into a boundary condition for $u=e^{x}$ gives $f(1)=e^{i\theta}f(0)$. Verify the boundary-condition family is exactly the family of self-adjoint extensions (the case $\theta=0$ is the periodic operator of the previous example).
items.axiom_audit: Inherits Countable Choice and Dependent Choice from the absolutely continuous calculus; the extension parameterization adds only AC through the deficiency-index machinery, which is not used quantitatively here.

items.title: An everywhere-defined closed operator on a Banach space is bounded
items.statement: Assume DC. Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces and let $T:X\to Y$ be linear and everywhere defined (so $D(T)=X$) with closed graph. Then $T$ is bounded. Consequently no unbounded closed operator, in particular no unbounded self-adjoint operator, can have domain all of $H$: self-adjoint unbounded operators have proper dense domains.
items.strategy: This is the closed graph theorem applied to the everywhere-defined operator $T$. The consequence for self-adjoint operators is immediate: a bounded self-adjoint operator is everywhere defined while an unbounded self-adjoint operator must have proper domain, so the resolvent identity and spectral theorem for unbounded operators are not rewritings of the bounded theory.
items.axiom_audit: Uses DC through the published closed graph theorem; declared.

items.title: A strongly continuous unitary group need not be norm continuous
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. On $H=L^2(\mathbb R)$ the unitary group $U(t)f(x)=e^{itx}f(x)$ is strongly continuous but not norm continuous: $\|U(t)-I\|=2$ for every $t\ne0$. Its generator $iQ$ (multiplication by $ix$ with domain $\{f:\int x^2|f|^2<\infty\}$) is unbounded, and a strongly continuous semigroup that is norm continuous at $0$ has a bounded generator.
items.strategy: Use dominated convergence for each orbit and normalized indicators of small finite intervals about pi/t for the exact norm lower bound. Identify generator iQ and test on indicators of [n,n+1] to prove it unbounded. For a general semigroup norm continuous at zero, construct the operator Riemann integral B_tau, invert B_tau/tau by a geometric series, and compute G B_tau=S(tau)-I, proving G bounded on the whole Banach space.
items.axiom_audit: Inherits AC from the generation lemma; the direct norm computation is choice-free.

items.title: Self-adjoint extensions and deficiency indices: agreement pointer
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. The extension theorem is proved on the A page: self-adjoint extensions of a closed symmetric operator correspond bijectively to the unitaries $K_+\to K_-$, and such a unitary exists exactly when the deficiency dimensions agree; the parameterization gives the exact domain and action, not merely a count. When a unitary is supplied, no further choice is used to produce the extension.
items.strategy: This remark is a pointer, not a proof: state the interface proved on the A page, warn that equal deficiency dimensions for finite $d_\pm$ do not by themselves exhibit the extension without the Hilbert-basis input recorded there, and note that the periodic operator of the examples is the case $\theta=0$.
items.axiom_audit: Inherits the choice principles declared on the A-page items it points to.
